I am not technical, and I am going to stop you the moment I stop understanding. How does it actually work?
Five steps. When a supplier file arrives, that triggers the process. Nobody presses anything.
And if the file is wrong? Because half of them are.
Then step two. The system reads nine fields, and if one of them is missing it flags the invoice instead of rejecting it. A person decides, not the system.
Which person? That matters more to me than the software.
Whoever you name. As soon as an invoice is flagged, one alert goes to that one person, with the invoice number in it. Step three: once they approve it, the two systems sync.
Is that immediate?

No, and I would rather be honest about it. It runs once a night, in one batch. If the run fails, we roll back and nothing half-finished reaches your ERP. Step five is the only one people ask about twice: every invoice can be traced from the supplier to the payment.

Once it is approved, the two systems sync overnight.

I have one test, and I apply it to every sentence I say in a customer meeting. Could this person repeat what I just said to somebody else, an hour from now, without me in the room? If the answer is no, then the sentence was mine and not theirs, and I have wasted it. What I have noticed over fifteen years is that the people who understand a system best use the fewest technical words. Jargon is almost always a place to hide. If somebody cannot tell me what happens when a file arrives, in ordinary language, I assume they have never watched it happen. And five steps is the limit. Not because people are slow, but because they are doing two things at the same time: following what you are saying, and deciding whether they trust you. Five steps, one verb each, is about as much as anybody can hold while doing both.

I sit through a lot of demos, and I want to say something that vendors find strange. I never need to know how it works. I need to know what happens when it does not work, and who finds out first. That is the whole thing. If a vendor tells me everything is in real time, I stop listening, because almost nothing is, and the sentence tells me they are repeating something they were given rather than describing a system they have watched. Say once a night and I believe the rest of it. And there is one question I ask that ends most demos. Show me what my team sees on a bad morning. Most people have no answer, because the demo was built for a good morning, and a good morning is not what I am buying insurance against.
